```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_orgdb <- requireNamespace("org.Hs.eg.db", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("org.Mm.eg.db", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_orgdb)
library(rsemverse)
```

This tutorial follows one analysis from the RSEM files to saved tables, using
the example that ships with the package. Every output below was produced when
this page was built. The example has three samples and 44 human genes; the
gene IDs are real Ensembl IDs and the expression values are synthetic, so the
numbers show how the function behaves, not biology.

## 1. Look at the input

```{r}
ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "rsemverse")
list.files(ex, recursive = TRUE)
```

The metadata lists each sample and the file that holds it:

```{r}
read.csv(file.path(ex, "metadata.csv"))
```

Each RSEM file is the usual gene-level output. These are the first rows of
sample `S1`, restricted to the columns that matter here:

```{r}
raw <- read.delim(
  file.path(ex, "data", "S1.genes.results"),
  colClasses = c(gene_id = "character")
)
head(raw[, c("gene_id", "expected_count", "TPM")], 4)
```

Note the version after the dot in `ENSG00000141510.5`. The OrgDb packages do
not know versions, and `rsem_read()` removes them for you.

## 2. Read the expected counts

```{r}
counts <- rsem_read(
  data     = file.path(ex, "data"),
  metadata = file.path(ex, "metadata.csv"),
  species  = "human",
  expr     = "count"
)
head(counts, 4)
```

The message reports `r nrow(raw)` genes in and `r nrow(counts)` rows out. The
result has one column per sample, in the order of `metadata.csv`:

```{r}
dim(counts)
colnames(counts)
```

## 3. Read the TPM

Change `expr` to get the TPM instead. Nothing else changes:

```{r}
tpm <- rsem_read(file.path(ex, "data"), file.path(ex, "metadata.csv"),
                 species = "human", expr = "tpm")
head(tpm, 4)
```

## 4. See what happened to the rows

**Rows that share a symbol are added.** In the example, two Ensembl IDs belong
to the gene `AAAS`:

```{r}
ids <- sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", raw$gene_id)
pair <- raw[ids %in% c("ENSG00000094914", "ENSG00000291836"),
            c("gene_id", "expected_count")]
pair
```

In the table they appear as one row, the sum of the two:

```{r}
counts["AAAS", "S1"]
sum(pair$expected_count)
```

**Genes without a symbol keep their ID.** Spike-ins and numeric IDs are not in
the OrgDb, so they stay as they were:

```{r}
kept <- rownames(counts)[rownames(counts) %in% raw$gene_id]
kept
```

**Nothing is lost.** Each column adds up to what it did in the file:

```{r}
all.equal(sum(counts$S1), sum(raw$expected_count))
all.equal(sum(tpm$S1), sum(raw$TPM))
```

Values are not rounded and TPM is not renormalized, so they are the numbers in
the RSEM files.

## 5. Save the tables

`rsem_read()` only returns a data frame. Saving is up to you:

```{r}
out_dir <- tempfile("tables-")
dir.create(out_dir)
write.csv(counts, file.path(out_dir, "count.csv"))
write.csv(tpm, file.path(out_dir, "tpm.csv"))
list.files(out_dir)
```

In the file, the gene symbols are in the first column, which has an empty
header. Read it back with the first column as row names:

```{r}
back <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "tpm.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
all.equal(back, tpm)
```

Use `check.names = FALSE` so that sample names such as `001` or `S-1` are not
changed on the way back.

## 6. A table for your own variable names

The data frame is yours: name it anything, and use it like any other data
frame.

```{r}
log2_tpm <- log2(tpm + 1)
top <- log2_tpm[order(-rowMeans(log2_tpm)), ][1:3, ]
round(top, 2)
```

```{r}
counts[c("TP53", "MYC"), ]
```

## 7. Mouse data

Use `species = "mouse"` for mouse data. To show it without extra files, this
step first writes a small mouse dataset (six genes plus a spike-in, two
samples) to a temporary folder, using mouse Ensembl IDs taken from
`org.Mm.eg.db`:

```{r}
symbols <- c("Trp53", "Actb", "Gapdh", "Myc", "Cd3e", "Pten")
ens <- suppressMessages(AnnotationDbi::mapIds(
  org.Mm.eg.db::org.Mm.eg.db, keys = symbols, keytype = "SYMBOL",
  column = "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first"
))
gene_id <- c(paste0(ens, ".", c(7, 15, 12, 20, 9, 14)), "ERCC-00002")

mouse_dir <- tempfile("mouse-")
dir.create(file.path(mouse_dir, "data"), recursive = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
for (s in c("M1", "M2")) {
  count <- round(rgamma(length(gene_id), shape = 2, rate = 0.02), 1)
  tab <- data.frame(
    gene_id = gene_id, `transcript_id(s)` = "T", length = 1000,
    effective_length = 800, expected_count = count,
    TPM = round(count / sum(count) * 1e6, 2), FPKM = 0, check.names = FALSE
  )
  write.table(tab, file.path(mouse_dir, "data", paste0(s, ".genes.results")),
              sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
}
writeLines(c("sample_id,ref", "M1,M1.genes.results", "M2,M2.genes.results"),
           file.path(mouse_dir, "metadata.csv"))
```

Now read it:

```{r}
mouse <- rsem_read(
  data     = file.path(mouse_dir, "data"),
  metadata = file.path(mouse_dir, "metadata.csv"),
  species  = "mouse",
  expr     = "count"
)
mouse
```

Mouse gene symbols are written in the mouse way (`Trp53`, not `TP53`). If you
give the wrong species, the function stops instead of returning a table full
of unannotated genes:

```{r, error = TRUE}
rsem_read(file.path(mouse_dir, "data"), file.path(mouse_dir, "metadata.csv"),
          species = "human", expr = "count")
```

## 8. Choosing and ordering samples

The metadata decides which samples are read and in which order. To analyse two
of the three example samples, in a different order, list only those:

```{r}
subset_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
writeLines(c("sample_id,ref", "S3,S3.genes.results", "S1,S1.genes.results"), subset_csv)

two <- rsem_read(file.path(ex, "data"), subset_csv, species = "human", expr = "tpm")
head(two, 3)
```

Files that are not listed are not read. This is also how you restrict the
analysis to one group of a larger experiment.

## What next

* [How it works](how-it-works.html) describes each rule and why it exists.
* [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html) lists the error messages.
* The result is a plain data frame, so it goes straight into your usual tools.
  Note that RSEM expected counts are not integers: tools that need integer
  counts (such as `DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromMatrix()`) need you to round them
  first, or you can use the `rsemflow` package, which reads RSEM files for
  DESeq2 through tximport.
